Title: England and Argentina fans gather in Atlanta with rivalries renewed for historic World Cup semi-final showdown
Chunks: 0,1,2,3,4,5,6
Hopes are high for another memorable match between two football powerhouses, whose previous encounters have included Diego Maradona's 'Hand of God' and David Beckham's red card.
Picture by Joel Barnett
Anticipation. Excitement. Tension. Three words that capture the mood in Atlanta, Georgia, as thousands of fans descend on the city ahead of the FIFA World Cup 2026 semi-final showdown between England andArgentina on Wednesday (15 July).
One of international football's fiercest rivalries,England and Argentina’s World Cup history is rich with unforgettable moments, from Diego Maradona's infamous 'Hand of God' goal to David Beckham's red card.
Yet their semi-final clash in Atlanta, USA, which also played host to the 1996 Olympic Games, will be just the sixth World Cup meeting between the two teams, and their first with a place in the final at stake.
Speaking to reporters in the mixed zone media area on the eve of the match, England defender **Marc Guéhi** told us, "Everyone’s excited."
**"You say the occasion, big players... everyone's relishing the opportunity** going into the game and [we're] looking forward to it," he added.
30 Jun 1998: David Beckham of England is sent off by referee Kim Nielsen after lashing out at Diego Simeone of Argentina #8 during the World Cup second round match at the Stade Geoffroy Guichard in St Etienne, France. England lost 4-3 on penalties as the ended 2-2 after extra-time \ Mandatory Credit: Ben Radford /Allsport
Among those looking forward to the match are Gabriel and his friend Frederico, who have arrived in Atlanta to show their support for their home nation, Argentina.
They have travelled from Tucumán, in the north of the country, and have seen the South American nation play against Egypt and Switzerland in the earlier rounds. Although they have been unable to secure tickets for Wednesday's semi-final, they said they were "really happy" to just be in the same city to cheer them on.
"The Argentina team is the best thing in our country," Gabriel told _Olympics.com_.
"It's something incredible. **We are very, very, very happy to be Argentinian. They represent us in the best way**. We're really happy to be here and supporting the team.

"I understand why we have that rivalry [with England], but it's like the players and the coach already said; this is football, and we are going to have fun, and we hope we win."
Picture by Getty Images
22 Jun 1986: Diego Maradona of Argentina handles the ball past Peter Shilton of England to score the opening goal of the World Cup Quarter Final at the Azteca Stadium in Mexico City, Mexico. Argentina won 2-1. (Photo by Bongarts/Getty Images)

### 'Robbery of the Century' and the 'Hand of God'
Widely regarded as the defining moment of their footballing rivalry, England and Argentina came head-to-head in the 1986 World Cup quarter-final at the Azteca Stadium in Mexico, a game forever associated with**Diego Maradona**'s two extraordinary goals.
His first, the infamous 'Hand of God', saw him controversially punch the ball into the net, a clear handball which wasn't spotted by the referee. The other, a breathtaking solo run from inside his own half, is considered one of the greatest goals ever scored.
Queuing to enter Atlanta's Centennial Olympic Park, which has been transformed into a FIFA Fanzone for the World Cup,was England fan Josan, and her husband, Sid, from Essex.
She remembers just how far the impact of Maradona's goals reached.
"**I wasn’t really into football that much** [in 1986], I probably read about it, but **everybody knew about it**," she told _Olympics.com_.
"There’s always so much weight on the players because of the history [of this fixture],"
This weight was no more evident than at the 1998 World Cup in Saint-Étienne, France, where England and Argentina faced each other in the Round of 16.
England’s 18-year-old striker Michael Owen announced himself on the world stage with a stunning individual goal, but the match turned early in the second half when David Beckham was bundled to the floor by Diego Simeone. The Englishman reacted, and was shown a red card for kicking out.
Reduced to 10 men, England eventually crashed out on penalties, with Beckham becoming the focus of national blame.
In a twist of fate, Diego Simeone’s son,Giuliano, was selected for the Argentina squad this time around and could feature against England on Wednesday.
In a Netflix documentary, _Beckham_, the former England captain reflected candidly on the moment and the years that followed.
"**I made a stupid mistake. It changed my life**," he said, before explaining how the moment led to an intense period of depression that lasted years. "As much as I don't like to talk about it... **I didn't eat, I didn't sleep. I was in a bad place**."

### 'Robbery of the Century' and the 'Hand of God'
30 Jun 1998: Michael Owen of England shrugs off Jose Chamot of Argentina on his way to goal during the World Cup second round match at the Stade Geoffroy Guichard in St Etienne, France. England lost 4-3 on penalties after a 2-2 draw. \ Mandatory Credit:Ross Kinnaird /Allsport
England fan Tihi Prpa instantly recalled "the David Beckham incident, with the kick out of the leg" when asked of his most memorable moment between the two sides, before adding: "and Michael Owen on the run."
Prpa, who was born in England in 1966, the year they last won the World Cup, received a ticket to Wednesday’s semi-final as a 60th birthday present from his sons, Aleksandar and Luka.
Waiting to enter the fanzone, he told _Olympics.com_: "I also remember the 'Hand of God', but then I also remember the run by Maradona.
"A lot of good memories and some bad memories, you know. But for England fans, not so many good ones there. They've had our number, let's put it that way."
"Hopefully this is going to be the time that, as everyone hopes, it's coming home," Prpa said.
Meanwhile, redemption for Beckham arrived only four years later.
Drawn together with Argentina in the group stage of the 2002 World Cup, England were awarded a first-half penalty after**Mauricio Pochettino**, now head coach of the US men's national team, fouled Owen inside the area.
Beckham stepped up and converted the spot-kick, sealing a famous 1-0 victory that finally exorcised some of the ghosts of 1998, and helped turn him into a national treasure.
Picture by 2005 Getty Images
German referee Rudolf Kreitlein sending off the Argentina captain Antonio Rattin during the World Cup match between England and Argentina at Wembley, 23rd July 1966. Rattin refused to leave the pitch and this confusion led to the use of red and yellow cards in football. (Photo by Central Press/Hulton Archive/Getty Images)

### Creation of the red and yellow cards
For Argentina, the sense of injustice stretches back to 1966, the year England won their only World Cup, during a game many in the country still refer to as _El Robo del Siglo_ ('The Robbery of the Century').
The two sides met in an ill-tempered quarter-final clash at Wembley Stadium, London, where Argentina captain **Antonio Rattin** was cautioned after tackling **Bobby Charlton**,before he was dismissed a few minutes later for dissent after protesting an earlier decision.
Rattin refused to leave the pitch initially and called for a translator, with Argentina's players insisting there had been a breakdown in communication. The standoff delayed the match by eight minutes and prompted English FIFA referee liaison Ken Aston to intervene.
Rattin was eventually escorted from the pitch by police officers, before he made one final gesture by sitting on the red carpet reserved for Queen Elizabeth II, drawing dismay from the home fans.
The incident led Aston to overhaul verbal cautions and introduce red and yellow cards, with them being handed out from the 1970 World Cup.
Despite committing 30 fouls and seeing striker **Geoff Hurst** escape a dismissal for an earlier challenge on **Roberto Ferreiro**, England went on to win 1-0 thanks to Hurst's headed winner.
Rattin died last Saturday, just hours before Argentina's quarter-final victory over Switzerland. Their players wore black armbands and held a moment of silence before the match in tribute to their former captain, who was aged 89.
Picture by 2026 Getty Images
KANSAS CITY, MISSOURI - JULY 11: Lionel Messi #10 and Julian Alvarez #9 of Argentina look on during the FIFA World Cup 2026 Quarter Final match between Argentina and Switzerland at Kansas City Stadium on July 11, 2026 in Kansas City, Missouri. (Photo by Carl Recine/Getty Images)

## Kane to make England history,Messi to play against Three Lions for first time
England captain Harry Kane will go head-to-head with Golden Boot rival Lionel Messi on Wednesday, and remarkably it will be the first time the Argentine superstar has ever played against the Three Lions.
The two sides last met in 2005 when Owen scored twice in a 3-2 victory for England. Messi had already made his senior international debut three months earlier against Hungary, but was given a red card two minutes later, meaning the 18-year-old was suspended for the England game.
Fast forward to 2026, and Argentina's captain arrives in Atlanta with eight goals at the tournament so far, two more than Kane, and leads the way in the all-time World Cup goalscorers' chart.
Yet despite the individual battle, the England captain insisted his side's focus is firmly on Argentina as a team rather than their prolific talisman.
"**We know how good a player he is**, we know what he’s done in the game, how consistent he’s been for so long,” Kane told _ITV Sport_.
"But **the game is against Argentina, not against Lionel Messi**. So yeah, we have a lot of preparation to do. We’re coming up against a great unit, a great team with fantastic players."

## Kane to make England history,Messi to play against Three Lions for first time
### Free-scoring Argentina
England’s task against the current world champions is daunting.
Argentina are looking to reach a third World Cup final in four tournaments and could become the first team to retain the trophy since Brazil in 1962.
_La Albiceleste_ (the white and sky blue) have been victorious in all five of their previous World Cup semi-finals and have won all their matches in this tournament so far, scoring 17 goals to move one goal behind their tournament record tally of 18, which they managed in the 1930 World Cup when they reached the final, but lost to Uruguay.
Each of their last four matches has seen them score three goals, and they could become the second team in history to score three goals in five consecutive games after France in 2022 and 2026.
Yet England defender Guéhi was unperturbed, and urged his teammates to play the "game of your life," to book a meeting against Spain in the final on Sunday.
"**There isn't pressure on us. What's the pressure?** The pressure, the onus is on them. **They're the world champions, so they need to come out**. They need to defend their title. So there's no pressure on us at all.
"Just make sure you're right for that game because it could be the game of your life. So **do what you can for your country. That's the message**."

England came away empty-handed at Wembley tonight after falling 3-2 to Spain in an intense five-goal clash.
​Lamine Yamal struck after just two minutes before Anthony Gordon and Harry Kane turned the match around before half-time. The turning point arrived early in the second half when Kane rattled the crossbar from the penalty spot and missed. Spain punished England ruthlessly, with Alex Baena levelling the score before Mikel Oyarzabal struck a 74th-minute winner to seal all three points for the world champions.

Hopes are high for another memorable match between two football powerhouses, whose previous encounters have included Diego Maradona's 'Hand of God' and David Beckham's red card.
Picture by Joel Barnett
Anticipation. Excitement. Tension. Three words that capture the mood in Atlanta, Georgia, as thousands of fans descend on the city ahead of the FIFA World Cup 2026 semi-final showdown between England andArgentina on Wednesday (15 July).
One of international football's fiercest rivalries,England and Argentina’s World Cup history is rich with unforgettable moments, from Diego Maradona's infamous 'Hand of God' goal to David Beckham's red card.
Yet their semi-final clash in Atlanta, USA, which also played host to the 1996 Olympic Games, will be just the sixth World Cup meeting between the two teams, and their first with a place in the final at stake.
Speaking to reporters in the mixed zone media area on the eve of the match, England defender **Marc Guéhi** told us, "Everyone’s excited."
**"You say the occasion, big players... everyone's relishing the opportunity** going into the game and [we're] looking forward to it," he added.
30 Jun 1998: David Beckham of England is sent off by referee Kim Nielsen after lashing out at Diego Simeone of Argentina #8 during the World Cup second round match at the Stade Geoffroy Guichard in St Etienne, France. England lost 4-3 on penalties as the ended 2-2 after extra-time \ Mandatory Credit: Ben Radford /Allsport
Among those looking forward to the match are Gabriel and his friend Frederico, who have arrived in Atlanta to show their support for their home nation, Argentina.
They have travelled from Tucumán, in the north of the country, and have seen the South American nation play against Egypt and Switzerland in the earlier rounds. Although they have been unable to secure tickets for Wednesday's semi-final, they said they were "really happy" to just be in the same city to cheer them on.
"The Argentina team is the best thing in our country," Gabriel told _Olympics.com_.
"It's something incredible. **We are very, very, very happy to be Argentinian. They represent us in the best way**. We're really happy to be here and supporting the team.

### 'Robbery of the Century' and the 'Hand of God'
Widely regarded as the defining moment of their footballing rivalry, England and Argentina came head-to-head in the 1986 World Cup quarter-final at the Azteca Stadium in Mexico, a game forever associated with**Diego Maradona**'s two extraordinary goals.
His first, the infamous 'Hand of God', saw him controversially punch the ball into the net, a clear handball which wasn't spotted by the referee. The other, a breathtaking solo run from inside his own half, is considered one of the greatest goals ever scored.
Queuing to enter Atlanta's Centennial Olympic Park, which has been transformed into a FIFA Fanzone for the World Cup,was England fan Josan, and her husband, Sid, from Essex.
She remembers just how far the impact of Maradona's goals reached.
"**I wasn’t really into football that much** [in 1986], I probably read about it, but **everybody knew about it**," she told _Olympics.com_.
"There’s always so much weight on the players because of the history [of this fixture],"
This weight was no more evident than at the 1998 World Cup in Saint-Étienne, France, where England and Argentina faced each other in the Round of 16.
England’s 18-year-old striker Michael Owen announced himself on the world stage with a stunning individual goal, but the match turned early in the second half when David Beckham was bundled to the floor by Diego Simeone. The Englishman reacted, and was shown a red card for kicking out.
Reduced to 10 men, England eventually crashed out on penalties, with Beckham becoming the focus of national blame.
In a twist of fate, Diego Simeone’s son,Giuliano, was selected for the Argentina squad this time around and could feature against England on Wednesday.
In a Netflix documentary, _Beckham_, the former England captain reflected candidly on the moment and the years that followed.
"**I made a stupid mistake. It changed my life**," he said, before explaining how the moment led to an intense period of depression that lasted years. "As much as I don't like to talk about it... **I didn't eat, I didn't sleep. I was in a bad place**."

### 'Robbery of the Century' and the 'Hand of God'
30 Jun 1998: Michael Owen of England shrugs off Jose Chamot of Argentina on his way to goal during the World Cup second round match at the Stade Geoffroy Guichard in St Etienne, France. England lost 4-3 on penalties after a 2-2 draw. \ Mandatory Credit:Ross Kinnaird /Allsport
England fan Tihi Prpa instantly recalled "the David Beckham incident, with the kick out of the leg" when asked of his most memorable moment between the two sides, before adding: "and Michael Owen on the run."
Prpa, who was born in England in 1966, the year they last won the World Cup, received a ticket to Wednesday’s semi-final as a 60th birthday present from his sons, Aleksandar and Luka.
Waiting to enter the fanzone, he told _Olympics.com_: "I also remember the 'Hand of God', but then I also remember the run by Maradona.
"A lot of good memories and some bad memories, you know. But for England fans, not so many good ones there. They've had our number, let's put it that way."
"Hopefully this is going to be the time that, as everyone hopes, it's coming home," Prpa said.
Meanwhile, redemption for Beckham arrived only four years later.
Drawn together with Argentina in the group stage of the 2002 World Cup, England were awarded a first-half penalty after**Mauricio Pochettino**, now head coach of the US men's national team, fouled Owen inside the area.
Beckham stepped up and converted the spot-kick, sealing a famous 1-0 victory that finally exorcised some of the ghosts of 1998, and helped turn him into a national treasure.

Rattin refused to leave the pitch and this confusion led to the use of red and yellow cards in football. (Photo by Central Press/Hulton Archive/Getty Images)

### Creation of the red and yellow cards
For Argentina, the sense of injustice stretches back to 1966, the year England won their only World Cup, during a game many in the country still refer to as _El Robo del Siglo_ ('The Robbery of the Century').
The two sides met in an ill-tempered quarter-final clash at Wembley Stadium, London, where Argentina captain **Antonio Rattin** was cautioned after tackling **Bobby Charlton**,before he was dismissed a few minutes later for dissent after protesting an earlier decision.
Rattin refused to leave the pitch initially and called for a translator, with Argentina's players insisting there had been a breakdown in communication. The standoff delayed the match by eight minutes and prompted English FIFA referee liaison Ken Aston to intervene.
Rattin was eventually escorted from the pitch by police officers, before he made one final gesture by sitting on the red carpet reserved for Queen Elizabeth II, drawing dismay from the home fans.
The incident led Aston to overhaul verbal cautions and introduce red and yellow cards, with them being handed out from the 1970 World Cup.
Despite committing 30 fouls and seeing striker **Geoff Hurst** escape a dismissal for an earlier challenge on **Roberto Ferreiro**, England went on to win 1-0 thanks to Hurst's headed winner.
Rattin died last Saturday, just hours before Argentina's quarter-final victory over Switzerland. Their players wore black armbands and held a moment of silence before the match in tribute to their former captain, who was aged 89.

KANSAS CITY, MISSOURI - JULY 11: Lionel Messi #10 and Julian Alvarez #9 of Argentina look on during the FIFA World Cup 2026 Quarter Final match between Argentina and Switzerland at Kansas City Stadium on July 11, 2026 in Kansas City, Missouri. (Photo by Carl Recine/Getty Images)

## Kane to make England history,Messi to play against Three Lions for first time
England captain Harry Kane will go head-to-head with Golden Boot rival Lionel Messi on Wednesday, and remarkably it will be the first time the Argentine superstar has ever played against the Three Lions.
The two sides last met in 2005 when Owen scored twice in a 3-2 victory for England. Messi had already made his senior international debut three months earlier against Hungary, but was given a red card two minutes later, meaning the 18-year-old was suspended for the England game.
Fast forward to 2026, and Argentina's captain arrives in Atlanta with eight goals at the tournament so far, two more than Kane, and leads the way in the all-time World Cup goalscorers' chart.
Yet despite the individual battle, the England captain insisted his side's focus is firmly on Argentina as a team rather than their prolific talisman.
"**We know how good a player he is**, we know what he’s done in the game, how consistent he’s been for so long,” Kane told _ITV Sport_.
"But **the game is against Argentina, not against Lionel Messi**. So yeah, we have a lot of preparation to do. We’re coming up against a great unit, a great team with fantastic players."

## Kane to make England history,Messi to play against Three Lions for first time
### Free-scoring Argentina
England’s task against the current world champions is daunting.
Argentina are looking to reach a third World Cup final in four tournaments and could become the first team to retain the trophy since Brazil in 1962.
_La Albiceleste_ (the white and sky blue) have been victorious in all five of their previous World Cup semi-finals and have won all their matches in this tournament so far, scoring 17 goals to move one goal behind their tournament record tally of 18, which they managed in the 1930 World Cup when they reached the final, but lost to Uruguay.
Each of their last four matches has seen them score three goals, and they could become the second team in history to score three goals in five consecutive games after France in 2022 and 2026.
Yet England defender Guéhi was unperturbed, and urged his teammates to play the "game of your life," to book a meeting against Spain in the final on Sunday.
"**There isn't pressure on us. What's the pressure?** The pressure, the onus is on them. **They're the world champions, so they need to come out**. They need to defend their title. So there's no pressure on us at all.
"Just make sure you're right for that game because it could be the game of your life. So **do what you can for your country. That's the message**."

England came away empty-handed at Wembley tonight after falling 3-2 to Spain in an intense five-goal clash.
​Lamine Yamal struck after just two minutes before Anthony Gordon and Harry Kane turned the match around before half-time. The turning point arrived early in the second half when Kane rattled the crossbar from the penalty spot and missed. Spain punished England ruthlessly, with Alex Baena levelling the score before Mikel Oyarzabal struck a 74th-minute winner to seal all three points for the world champions.

**Paris Match Is Easy For Chelsea(Sky Sports)**
**Paris Saint Germain 0 Chelsea 3**
Jose Mourinho was prepared to accept a point, but Chelsea earned all three with a minimum of fuss as Paris Saint Germain were beaten 3-0 in the Parc des Princes.
Didier Drogba settled victory on the stroke of half time, adding to John Terry's 29th-minute header, and garnished it with a sublime but superfluous third.
Mourinho's previous UEFA Champions League match was the 2004 final. The seamless transition from Porto to Chelsea continued with another comprehensive disection of French opposition.
Their efficiency was exemplified by Terry's opener, the captain heading in Frank Lampard's corner while Lionel Letizi clawed at thin air.
When Joe Cole sent substitute Mateja Kezman scurrying through on goal, the keeper redeemed himself with a point-blank block only for Drogba to sidefoot home the rebound. The 24 million striker has a solitary goal to show for five Premiership appearances, but a return to French soil reignited his scoring instincts and his second-half free kick left Letizi motionless.
It was dispatched with a delicacy which Drogba's early appearances in English football have not revealed. Still more surprising was a Veronesque flick behind his standing foot that almost provided Tiago with an opportunity to open the scoring.
But the first flourish came from Charles-Edouard Coridon, who left Terry on his backside with a weaving solo run, culminating in a shot wide. It promised more than PSG delivered.

Chelsea's organisation restricted them to long-range shots. Pauleta and Jerome Rothen shot wide but Modeste M'Bami at least tested the athletic Petr Cech.
Drogba was busier, heading straight at Letizi from a Lampard free kick. His set-piece expertise was confirmed by Terry's opener and Lampard, with impressive maturity, controlled the midfield, forsaking his trademark forward runs to prompt his two strikers and Cole with a series of inviting passes.
And the inventive Cole was the instigator of the second, a perfectly-weighted pass exploiting the lack of pace in the Paris defence. He almost joined Drogba on the scoresheet, displaying the tecnhique to test Letizi from an acute angle, but not the control to take advantage of Lampard's chipped pass.
The persistent Pauleta responded with two low shots Cech held, but the dominant Drogba reiterated Chelsea's superiority in some style. The former Marseille man's popularity in Paris plummeted further with a departing salute to the home fans but his manager, who invariably appears impervious to public opinion, now has five wins and as many clean sheets in six games.
